questions.q: Why is 'it works' at prototype scale not the same claim as 'it works in production at scale'?
options: Scale only ever changes the user interface, never the underlying architecture
There is no real difference -- a working prototype guarantees production readiness

New failure modes, costs, and load behaviors can appear at scale that were structurally impossible to encounter at prototype scale, so prototype success proves the approach is sound but not that it will hold up in production
Prototype code and production code are always written in different programming languages
questions.explain: Scaling isn't 'the same system, but bigger' -- it introduces genuinely new failure modes (partial outages, cost at volume, organizational dependencies) that a small-scale prototype never has to face.

questions.q: Why does a per-request cost that was 'invisible' at prototype scale become a major concern at production scale?
options: Costs only matter once a system is open-sourced
Because that small cost gets multiplied by real production volume, turning a negligible number into a significant, sometimes board-level budget line
Production systems are legally required to report costs, unlike prototypes
Per-request costs are always identical regardless of how many requests are made
questions.explain: A fraction-of-a-cent API call is irrelevant at ten requests a day and can become a dominant cost line at millions of requests -- the per-request economics don't change, but their real-world impact does.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say that at large scale, 'some component is statistically always degraded somewhere'?
options: This is only true for systems that have never been properly tested
Large-scale systems are inherently built with worse code than small-scale ones
Degradation only happens during planned maintenance windows
With enough dependent services and enough raw request volume, partial failure becomes a continuous condition to design around, not a rare edge case to react to after the fact
questions.explain: At small scale, a dependency outage is a rare event; at large scale with enough moving parts, partial degradation becomes a near-constant background condition the architecture must tolerate continuously.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the Staff/Principal engineer's highest-leverage output, as distinct from a junior or mid-level engineer's?
options: Writing more lines of code per day than anyone else on the team
Working exclusively on the most technically difficult parts of the codebase
Avoiding all meetings and discussions with other teams
Often a decision, written down (e.g., an architecture choice and its reasoning) that other engineers can act on without re-litigating it, rather than code itself
questions.explain: The shift at this level is toward decisions and documentation that other engineers can build on confidently, not just more code -- exactly what Chapter 2's lessons on architecture decision records are about.

questions.q: What is Northbeam, as used in this chapter?
options: The name of a specific vector database product
A real, named company whose actual internal engineering decisions are being disclosed
An unrelated marketing exercise with no connection to the lesson content
A fictional but realistic composite company whose scaling RAG assistant is used as a running case study across the chapter's lessons
questions.explain: Northbeam is explicitly introduced as a fictional composite used to make the chapter's architecture decisions concrete and realistic, not a real company or product being described.
